item.dc:creator: Kunlun Zhu, Hongyi Du, Zhaochen Hong, Xiaocheng Yang, Shuyi Guo, Zhe Wang, Zhenhailong Wang, Cheng Qian, Xiangru Tang, Heng Ji, Jiaxuan You

item.title: Reinforcement Learning with Reference-Based Rewards for Language Model Reasoning and Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2504.09895v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) powers two major lines of large language model (LLM) post-training: reasoning, which elicits deliberate, verifiable problem solving, and alignment, which steers models toward helpful, harmless, and honest behavior. Both hinge on reward design. Reasoning relies on rule-based verification of final answers, whose binary feedback is blind to intermediate derivations, whereas process reward models (PRMs) require step-level annotations too costly to scale. Alignment depends on reward models (RMs) trained on binary preference pairs, making both data collection and model training resource-intensive. We propose RL2R, reinforcement learning with reference-based rewards, as a unified and inexpensive alternative. Using pre-existing or distilled references, RL2R measures semantic similarity with lightweight metrics such as BERTScore between a sampled generation and a reference answer or solution. Similarity preserves ordinal quality signals that binary feedback discards: responses closer to the reference earn higher rewards, and sound derivations receive credit even when the final conclusion is wrong. For mathematical reasoning, augmenting rule-based verification with answer- and step-level similarity provides low-cost process supervision and outperforms answer-only verification. For alignment, a critic-free REINFORCE-style instantiation covers general preference, safety, and confidence tasks on par with RM-based methods. Reference-based rewards thus offer a cost-effective, versatile reward source spanning reasoning and alignment.
item.dc:creator: Shuai Zhao, Yunqiu Xu, Linchao Zhu, Ling Chen, Yi Yang

item.title: FedS2R: One-Shot Federated Domain Generalization for Synthetic-to-Real Semantic Segmentation in Autonomous Driving
item.description: arXiv:2507.19881v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Federated domain generalization has shown promising progress in image classification by enabling collaborative training across multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, its potential in the semantic segmentation of autonomous driving remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose FedS2R, the first one-shot federated domain generalization framework for synthetic-to-real semantic segmentation in autonomous driving. FedS2R comprises two components: an inconsistency-driven data augmentation strategy that generates images for unstable classes, and a multi-client knowledge distillation scheme with feature fusion that distills a global model from multiple client models. Experiments on five real-world datasets, Cityscapes, BDD100K, Mapillary, IDD, and ACDC, show that the global model significantly outperforms individual client models and is only 2 mIoU points behind the model trained with simultaneous access to all client data. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of FedS2R in synthetic-to-real semantic segmentation for autonomous driving under federated learning
item.dc:creator: Tao Lian, Jose L. G\'omez, Antonio M. L\'opez

item.title: How K-12 Teachers Adapt Generative AI to Local Classroom Demands: Cultural Distance Between GenAI Defaults and Everyday Teaching Practices
item.description: arXiv:2509.10780v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is entering K-12 classrooms, but its default culture does not always fit local teaching. Existing accounts either treat this misfit as macro-level structural bias or examine it through single-case studies; neither captures how much work teachers must do to make outputs usable across tasks. This exploratory, theory-building qualitative study introduces cultural distance, the gap between GenAI's default cultural repertoire and the situated demands of teachers' practice. Through interviews with 30 K-12 teachers who frequently use GenAI, 10 each from South Africa, Taiwan, and the United States, we identified three levels defined by the effort teachers invested and whether it yielded a usable output: low (minor edits), mid (sustained prompting and revision), and high (structural gaps rooted in unsupported languages, undigitized knowledge, or policy filters that no teacher effort can close). We present cultural distance as a promising framework requiring further examination and draw implications for designers, policymakers, and educators.
item.dc:creator: Qing Xiao, Ruiwei Xiao, Hanqi Jane Li, Phenyo Phemelo Moletsane, Xinying Hou, John Stamper, Hong Shen

item.title: Improving Outdoor Multi-cell Fingerprinting-based Positioning via Mobile Data Augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2509.19405v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate outdoor positioning in cellular networks is hindered by sparse, heterogeneous measurement collections and the high cost of exhaustive site surveys. This paper introduces a lightweight, modular mobile data augmentation framework designed to enhance multi-cell fingerprinting-based positioning using operator-collected minimization of drive test (MDT) records. The proposed approach decouples spatial and radio-feature synthesis: kernel density estimation (KDE) models the empirical spatial distribution to generate geographically coherent synthetic locations, while a 1-nearest-neighbor (1NN)-based block produces augmented per-cell radio fingerprints. The architecture is intentionally training-free, interpretable, and suitable for distributed or on-premise operator deployments, supporting privacy-aware workflows. We both validate each augmentation module independently and assess its end-to-end impact on fingerprinting-based positioning using a real-world MDT dataset provided by an Italian mobile network operator across diverse urban and peri-urban scenarios. Results show that the proposed KDE-1NN augmentation consistently improves positioning performance with respect to state-of-the-art approaches, reducing the median positioning error by up to 30% (specifically achieved at an augmentation rate of x30 in the highly sparse highway scenario). We also observe region-dependent saturation effects, which emerge most rapidly in scenarios with high user density where the information gain from additional synthetic samples quickly diminishes. Overall, the framework offers a practical, low-complexity path to enhance operator positioning services using existing mobile data traces.
item.dc:creator: Tony Chahoud, Lorenzo Mario Amorosa, Riccardo Marini, Luca De Nardis

item.title: MonitorVLM:A Vision Language Framework for Safety Violation Detection in Mining Operations
item.description: arXiv:2510.03666v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Industrial accidents, particularly in high-risk domains such as surface and underground mining, are frequently caused by unsafe worker behaviors. Traditional manual inspection remains labor-intensive, error-prone, and insufficient for large-scale, dynamic environments, highlighting the urgent need for intelligent and automated safety monitoring. In this paper, we present MonitorVLM, a novel vision--language framework designed to detect safety violations directly from surveillance video streams. MonitorVLM introduces three key innovations: (1) a domain-specific violation dataset comprising 9,000 vision--question--answer (VQA) samples across 40 high-frequency mining regulations, enriched with augmentation and auxiliary detection cues; (2) a clause filter (CF) module that dynamically selects the Top-$K$ most relevant clauses, reducing inference latency by 13.56% while maintaining accuracy; and (3) a behavior magnifier (BM) module that enhances worker regions to improve fine-grained action recognition, yielding additional gains of 3.45% in precision and 8.62% in recall. Experimental results demonstrate that MonitorVLM significantly outperforms baseline vision--language models, achieving improvements of 22.01% in precision, 34.22\% in recall, and 28.37% in F1 score over the 72B unfine-tuned baseline. A lightweight web-based interface further integrates MonitorVLM into practical workflows, enabling automatic violation reporting with video timestamping. This study highlights the potential of multimodal large models to enhance occupational safety monitoring in mining and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Jiang Wu, Sichao Wu, Yinsong Ma, Guangyuan Yu, Haoyuan Xu, Lifang Zheng, Jingliang Duan

item.title: TinyMyo: a Tiny Foundation Model for Flexible EMG Signal Processing at the Edge
item.description: arXiv:2512.15729v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Objective: Surface electromyography (EMG) is widely used in biomechanics, rehabilitation, prosthetic control, and human-machine interfaces. Generalization across subjects, recording systems, and acquisition protocols remains challenging. Existing EMG foundation models (FMs) have limited support for multiple downstream tasks and deployment on low-power devices. Methods: We introduce TinyMyo, a 3.6-million-parameter Transformer encoder pre-trained on public EMG datasets using self-supervised masked reconstruction. TinyMyo supports multiple tasks with minimal changes to the task-specific prediction head. Results: We evaluated TinyMyo on hand gesture classification, hand kinematic regression, speech production, and speech recognition. For gesture classification, TinyMyo outperformed previously reported EMG FMs, achieving accuracies of 87.98% on NinaPro DB5, 97.1% on UCI-EMG, and 96.6% on EPN-612. On the GAP9 ultra-low-power microcontroller, TinyMyo achieved an inference time of 0.785 s and consumed 44.91 mJ per inference at an average power of 57.18 mW. A 1.9-million-parameter variant processed 5 s and 1 s input windows in 0.496 s and 0.089 s, respectively. Conclusion: TinyMyo demonstrates that a compact, self-supervised EMG encoder can support multiple downstream tasks and run on a low-power microcontroller. Significance: To our knowledge, this is the first deployment of an EMG FM on an ultra-low-power microcontroller, opening a path to on-device motor intent decoding, neuromuscular assessment, and human-machine interaction.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Fasulo, Giusy Spacone, Thorir Mar Ingolfsson, Yawei Li, Luca Benini, Andrea Cossettini

item.title: Meta-RL with Bayesian Linear Task Models
item.description: arXiv:2512.20974v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep Bayesian reinforcement learning adapts to unseen tasks by inferring latent transition and reward models, but existing methods typically rely on variational posteriors and evidence lower bounds, introducing approximation error and unstable task representations. We introduce GLiBRL, a deep Bayesian RL framework that combines generalised linear task models with learnable non-linear basis functions. GLiBRL features conjugate Bayesian inference, yielding exact, sequential posterior updates over task parameters and model noise, together with a closed-form marginal likelihood that eliminates variational inference. The update is naturally permutation-invariant, allowing GLiBRL to integrate with both off- and on-policy algorithms. GLiBRL also learns task representation admitting an exact kernel identity, relating distances between task representations to kernel discrepancies over the task contexts. Compared against eight representative or recent meta reinforcement learning methods, GLiBRL achieves the highest aggregate zero-shot test performance on both the MuJoCo locomotion and MetaWorld manipulation benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Jingyang You, Hanna Kurniawati

item.title: Low-Dimensional Adaptation of Rectified Flow: A Diffusion and Stochastic Localization Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2601.15500v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In recent years, Rectified flow (RF) has gained considerable popularity largely due to its generation efficiency and state-of-the-art performance. In this paper, we investigate how well RF automatically adapts to the intrinsic low dimensionality of the support of the target distribution to accelerate sampling. We show that, using a carefully designed end-point adapted time-discretization scheme and with sufficiently accurate drift estimates, the RF sampler enjoys an iteration complexity of order $O(k/\varepsilon)$ (up to log factors), where $\varepsilon$ is the precision in total variation distance and $k$ is the intrinsic dimension of the target distribution. In addition, we show that the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) procedure is equivalent to a stochastic version of RF by establishing a novel connection between these processes and stochastic localization. Building on this connection, we further design a stochastic RF sampler that also adapts to the low-dimensionality of the target distribution under mild requirements on the accuracy of the drift estimates, and also with a specific time schedule. We illustrate the efficacy of newly designed time-discretization schedules with simulations on the synthetic data and text-to-image (T2I) data experiments.
item.dc:creator: Saptarshi Roy, Alessandro Rinaldo, Purnamrita Sarkar

item.title: Disentangling generalization and memorization in large language models using chess
item.description: arXiv:2601.16823v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities, yet it remains unclear to what extent these reflect sophisticated recall or genuine reasoning ability. We introduce chess as a controlled testbed aimed at disentangling these faculties. Leveraging the game's structure and scalable engine evaluations, we construct a taxonomy of positions varying in density of relevant priors -- ranging from common states solvable by memorization to completely novel ones requiring generalization. Crucially, our approach achieves this distinction without requiring explicit knowledge of the models' training data. Applying this taxonomy, we combine a longitudinal analysis of the GPT lineage with a rigorous evaluation of contemporary models, including Claude Opus and Gemini. Our analysis reveals a steep gradient: performance consistently degrades as the density of relevant priors decreases. Notably, for tasks with few relevant priors, base model performance regresses to the random-play baseline, and all models propose illegal moves at sharply increasing rates, indicating that they fail to reliably apply the fixed rules of the game in unfamiliar positions. While newer models improve, progress slows significantly for tasks with sparse priors. Furthermore, while reasoning-augmented inference improves performance, its relative marginal benefit per token decreases in the absence of relevant priors. These results suggest limitations in systematic generalization, highlighting the need for mechanisms beyond scale to achieve robust performance when deprived of relevant priors.
item.dc:creator: Leonard S. Pleiss, Maximilian Schiffer, Robert K. von Weizsaecker

item.title: CoreQ: Mismatch-Corrected Successive Rounding for LLM Quantization
item.description: arXiv:2602.05902v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) enables efficient deployment of large language models by mapping pretrained weights to low-bit formats without retraining, typically using a small calibration set to minimize a layer-wise calibration objective. However, this sequential procedure induces a mismatch: errors from earlier quantized layers alter the inputs received by later layers, causing the activations to deviate from those of the full-precision model. Recent approaches introduce mismatch-aware calibration objectives to compensate for this effect, but leave open how much of the observed mismatch should shift each layer's calibration target. We show that fully applying the empirical mismatch correction can overfit finite calibration data, while using a fixed correction coefficient ignores variation in mismatch estimates across layers. To address these limitations, we propose CoreQ, a learning-free PTQ framework that uses a geometric decomposition of the mismatch to compute a closed-form, layer-adaptive correction coefficient. This coefficient controls how much of the observed mismatch enters each layer's calibration target, reducing overfitting to limited calibration data without coefficient tuning. CoreQ then applies efficient greedy successive rounding to the resulting triangular least-squares objective. Its bounded beam-search extension, K-CoreQ, trades modest additional compute for improved performance. Across multiple LLM families, scales, bit-widths, and quantization settings, CoreQ and K-CoreQ achieve lower perplexity and higher downstream accuracy than strong PTQ baselines. Code is available at GitHub.
item.dc:creator: Seohyeon Cha, Huancheng Chen, Dongjun Kim, Haoran Zhang, Kevin Chan, Gustavo de Veciana, Haris Vikalo

item.title: PANC: Prior-Aware Normalized Cut for Training-Free In-Context Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2602.06912v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study training-free in-context segmentation with externally annotated context priors: given a target image and a small set of foreground/background tokens extracted from annotated context images, the goal is to segment the corresponding target concept without training, fine-tuning, or target-image clicks. Existing ViT-token spectral methods such as TokenCut are class-agnostic and can select the wrong object in multi-object scenes, or become unstable in low-semantic texture-dominated domains. We propose PANC, a prior-aware spectral segmentation pipeline that injects external labeled tokens into a frozen ViT affinity graph through two foreground/background anchor nodes. The anchors do not clamp target-image tokens; instead, they softly bias the Normalized Cut eigenspace while preserving the target-image affinity structure. PANC further uses prior-aware sign stabilization and prior-driven thresholding to obtain deterministic masks. Across heterogeneous saliency datasets and homogeneous low-semantic domains, PANC improves over architecture-matched no-prior token-graph baselines, with the largest gains in settings where class-agnostic saliency is ambiguous or weak.
item.dc:creator: Juan Guti\'errez, Victor Guti\'errez-Garc\'ia, Jos\'e Luis Blanco-Murillo

item.title: Generating Adversarial Events: A Motion-Aware Point Cloud Framework
item.description: arXiv:2602.08230v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Event cameras have been widely adopted in safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving, robotics, and human-computer interaction. A pressing challenge arises from the vulnerability of deep neural networks to adversarial examples, which poses a significant threat to the reliability of event-based systems. Nevertheless, research into adversarial attacks on events is scarce. This is primarily due to the non-differentiable nature of mainstream event representations, which hinders the extension of gradient-based attack methods. In this paper, we propose MA-ADV, a novel \textbf{M}otion-\textbf{A}ware \textbf{Adv}ersarial framework. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to generate adversarial events by leveraging point cloud representations. MA-ADV accounts for high-frequency noise in events and employs a diffusion-based approach to smooth perturbations, while fully leveraging the spatial and temporal relationships among events. Finally, MA-ADV identifies the minimal-cost perturbation through a combination of sample-wise Adam optimization, iterative refinement, and binary search. Extensive experimental results validate that MA-ADV ensures a 100\% attack success rate with minimal perturbation cost, and also demonstrate enhanced robustness against defenses, underscoring the critical security challenges facing future event-based perception systems.
item.dc:creator: Hongwei Ren, Lansong Yang, Youxin Jiang, Tuopusen Huang, Xiangqian Wu

item.title: Multimodal Information Fusion for Chart Understanding: A Survey of MLLMs -- Evolution, Limitations, and Cognitive Enhancement
item.description: arXiv:2602.10138v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chart understanding is a quintessential information fusion task, requiring the seamless integration of graphical and textual data to extract meaning. The advent of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has revolutionized this domain, yet the landscape of MLLM-based chart analysis remains fragmented and lacks systematic organization. This survey provides a comprehensive roadmap of this nascent frontier by structuring the domain's core components. We begin by analyzing the fundamental challenges of fusing visual and linguistic information in charts. We then categorize downstream tasks and datasets, introducing a novel taxonomy of canonical and non-canonical benchmarks to highlight the field's expanding scope. Subsequently, we present a comprehensive evolution of methodologies, tracing the progression from classic deep learning techniques to state-of-the-art MLLM paradigms that leverage sophisticated fusion strategies. By critically examining the limitations of current models, particularly their perceptual and reasoning deficits, we identify promising future directions, including advanced alignment techniques and reinforcement learning for cognitive enhancement. This survey aims to equip researchers and practitioners with a structured understanding of how MLLMs are transforming chart information fusion and to catalyze progress toward more robust and reliable systems.
item.dc:creator: Zhihang Yi, Jian Zhao, Jiancheng Lv, Tao Wang

item.title: Colosseum: Auditing Collusion in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2602.15198v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems, where LLM agents communicate through free-form language, enable sophisticated coordination for solving complex cooperative tasks. This surfaces a unique safety problem when a group of agents forms a coalition and colludes to pursue secondary goals and degrade the joint objective. In this paper, we present Colosseum, a framework for auditing LLM agents' collusive behavior in multi-agent settings. We ground how agents cooperate through a formal multi-agent decision-making framework and measure action-based collusive behavior in actions via regret relative to the cooperative optimum and compare it with communication-based collusive behavior. Colosseum enables audits of LLM agents for collusion under benign settings, different coalition objectives, persuasion tactics, and network topologies. We then introduce a new behavioral probe by creating secret communication channels between agents, showing that most out-of-the-box models exhibit a propensity to collude under this probe, which we term emergent collusion. Furthermore, we discover ``collusion on paper'' when agents plan to collude in text but often pick non-collusive actions. Colosseum provides a new way to audit collusion in cooperative multi-agent systems while presenting observations about how collusion emerges, what affects collusion efficacy, and which strategies may mitigate it.
item.dc:creator: Mason Nakamura, Abhinav Kumar, Saswat Das, Sahar Abdelnabi, Saaduddin Mahmud, Ferdinando Fioretto, Shlomo Zilberstein, Eugene Bagdasarian

item.title: Counterfactual Feature Regularization for Expansion-Based Class-Incremental Learning
item.description: arXiv:2603.09145v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Current expansion-based methods for Class Incremental Learning (CIL) effectively mitigate catastrophic forgetting by freezing old features. However, such task-specific features learned from the new task may collide with the old features. From a causal perspective, spurious feature correlations are the main cause of this collision, manifesting in two scopes: (i) guided by empirical risk minimization (ERM), intra-task spurious correlations cause task-specific features to rely on shortcut features. These non-robust features are vulnerable to interference, inevitably drifting into the feature space of other tasks; (ii) inter-task spurious correlations induce semantic confusion between visually similar classes across tasks. To address this, we propose a Probability of Necessity and Sufficiency (PNS)-based regularization method to guide feature expansion in CIL. Specifically, we first extend the definition of PNS to expansion-based CIL, termed CPNS, which quantifies both the causal completeness of intra-task representations and the separability of inter-task representations. We then introduce a dual-scope counterfactual generator based on twin networks to ensure the measurement of CPNS, which simultaneously generates: (i) intra-task counterfactual features to minimize intra-task PNS risk and ensure causal completeness of task-specific features, and (ii) inter-task interfering features to minimize inter-task PNS risk, ensuring the separability of inter-task representations. Theoretical analyses confirm its reliability. The regularization is a plug-and-play method for expansion-based CIL to mitigate feature collision. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Zhen Zhang, Jielei Chu, Jiangtao Hu, Bin Liu, Jie Wang, Ya Liu, Fengmao Lv, Tianrui Li

item.title: SHAMISA: SHAped Modeling of Implicit Structural Associations for Self-supervised No-Reference Image Quality Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2603.13669v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: No-Reference Image Quality Assessment (NR-IQA) aims to estimate perceptual quality without access to a pristine reference. Learning an NR-IQA model faces a fundamental bottleneck because it requires many costly human perceptual labels. We propose SHAMISA, a non-contrastive self-supervised framework that learns from unlabeled distorted images through explicitly structured relational supervision. Unlike prior methods that impose rigid binary similarity constraints, SHAMISA shapes soft, controllable implicit structural associations that are both distortion-aware and content-sensitive. A key innovation is its compositional distortion engine, which generates an uncountable family of degradations from continuous parameter spaces and groups the resulting images so that exactly one distortion factor varies at a time. This construction enables fine-grained control over representational similarity during training. Images with shared distortion patterns are pulled together in the embedding space, while severity variations produce structured shifts. Dual-source relation graphs integrate known degradation profiles with emergent structural affinities throughout pre-training. The learned encoder is then frozen and paired with a linear regressor. Extensive experiments on synthetic, authentic, and cross-dataset NR-IQA benchmarks demonstrate strong overall performance, improved transfer in the reported cross-dataset comparisons, and favorable qualitative robustness diagnostics. Self-supervised pre-training requires no IQA opinion-score annotations or contrastive loss.
item.dc:creator: Mahdi Naseri, Zhou Wang

item.title: Auditing Path-Specific Fairness Across Causal Discovery Algorithms: A Heart Failure Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2603.15926v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Causal discovery is increasingly applied to healthcare data, where the recovered relationships can encode biased pathways that propagate to downstream prediction. Path-specific fairness analysis, through direct, indirect, and spurious effect decompositions along with fairness-utility ratio assessment allows bias quantification and associated prediction cost. However, existing evaluations of causal discovery under fairness constraints have largely used non-clinical datasets and have not separated the contribution of confounders from that of mediators, leaving open how discovery-algorithm choice propagates through path-specific fairness to the utility trade-off in clinical settings. This work addresses that gap by establishing an expert-elicited causal graph benchmark for the heart failure clinical records dataset and tracing discovery algorithms through composite, per-variable fairness decompositions and fairness-utility ratio. ICA-LiNGAM achieves the lowest structural Hamming distance and highest recall, while GES achieves the highest precision. For path-specific effects, there was a 1.2 percentage-point difference in the mediated effect on ejection fraction on overall causal fairness between the original and discovered graphs. This ultimately led to variations in the fairness-utility ratio highlighting need for fine-grained evaluation. These results indicate that discovery-aware, path-specific fairness evaluation is consequential in clinical settings and warrants inclusion in routine auditing of clinical risk models.
item.dc:creator: Nitish Nagesh, Elahe Khatibi, Thomas Hughes, Mahdi Bagheri, Pratik Gajane, Amir M. Rahmani

item.title: Knowledge Localization in Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Using Cross-Lingual Inconsistency
item.description: arXiv:2603.17102v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern LLMs continue to exhibit significant variance in behavior across languages, such as being able to recall factual information in some languages but not others. While typically studied as a problem to be mitigated, in this work, we propose leveraging this cross-lingual inconsistency as a tool for interpretability in mixture-of-experts (MoE) LLMs. Our knowledge localization framework contrasts routing for sets of languages where the model correctly recalls information from languages where it fails. This allows us to isolate model components that play a functional role in answering about a piece of knowledge. Our method proceeds in two stages: (1) querying the model with difficult factual questions across a diverse set of languages to generate "success" and "failure" activation buckets and then (2) applying a statistical contrastive analysis to the MoE router logits to identify experts important for knowledge. To validate the necessity of this small number of experts for answering a knowledge question, we deactivate them and re-ask the question. We find that despite only deactivating about 20 out of 6000 experts, the model no longer answers correctly in over 40% of cases. Generally, this method provides a realistic and scalable knowledge localization approach to address increasingly complex LLMs.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Bandarkar, Alan Ansell, Trevor Cohn

item.title: HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2603.19008v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves Large Language Models (LLMs) by grounding generation in external, non-parametric knowledge. However, when a task requires choosing among competing possibilities, such as a diagnosis among plausible alternatives, topically relevant context is often insufficient to drive the final decision. To address this issue, we propose HYPER: Hypothesis-Guided Planning for Evidence-Seeking Retrieval, a training-free pre-retrieval planning framework that reorients RAG from topic-oriented retrieval to evidence-oriented retrieval. HYPER uses a provisional answer hypothesis as a planning anchor. It then decomposes retrieval into three evidence roles. Support seeks evidence for the provisional answer. Distinction retrieves criteria that separate competing alternatives. Feature grounds salient question features needed for the decision. This planning step steers retrieval toward evidence near the decision boundary, enabling the generator to answer from context that is more directly aligned with the required choice. On MedQA and MMLU-Med, where single-query retrieval falls below no-retrieval chain-of-thought prompting, HYPER achieves the best average accuracy among ten baselines, improving over Simple RAG by 5.9 and 3.6 points, respectively. Its gains transfer to the 14 subjects of MMLU-Pro, at the cost of two additional LLM calls per question. Code is available at https://github.com/hangeol/HypothesisRAG.
item.dc:creator: Hangeol Chang, Changsun Lee, Seungjoon Rho, Junho Yeo, Jong Chul Ye

item.title: PEARL: Personalized Streaming Video Understanding with Runtime-Defined Concepts
item.description: arXiv:2603.20422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unlike humans, who learn new concepts from a continuous visual stream, existing personalized vision-language models (VLMs) internalize a predefined concept set during training and operate on static images or offline videos. They cannot register a concept that a user defines in the middle of a stream, nor recall the earlier moments in which it appeared. We formalize this task as Personalized Streaming Video Understanding (PSVU) and introduce PSVU-Bench, the first benchmark for this task, which annotates 132 videos with timestamped questions. Its Concept-Definition, Real-Time and Past-Time QA ask a model to register concepts at arbitrary timestamps, recognize their current state, including user-defined actions, and retrieve their historical evidence. We propose PEARL, a strong plug-and-play baseline that stores user-defined concepts apart from archived video clips and rewrites each query with concept descriptions to retrieve the relevant history. Grounding a named concept in video is a skill shared by all concepts. We therefore construct PSVU-10K, a training set of verified concept questions on public internet videos, and train the retriever and answering VLM of PEARL on it once. Concepts defined at test time still require no training. Applied to three architectures without training, PEARL improves Real-Time QA by 15.05% and Past-Time QA by 12.60% on average over the corresponding offline models, and all three surpass existing online video models on both QA types. Training further improves PEARL on Qwen3-VL-8B by 8.66% on Real-Time QA and 9.39% on Past-Time QA, with gains in every category. Code, data and models are available at https://github.com/Yuanhong-Zheng/PEARL.
item.dc:creator: Yuanhong Zheng, Ruichuan An, Xiaopeng Lin, Yuxing Liu, Sihan Yang, Huanyu Zhang, Haodong Li, Qintong Zhang, Renrui Zhang, Guopeng Li, Yifan Zhang, Yuheng Li, Wentao Zhang

item.title: Reading Human Preference from Looped Transformer Internal States
item.description: arXiv:2604.09870v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Show a frozen language model two replies to the same request, one of which a person preferred. Can a small probe on the model's hidden states tell which? On Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, a model that runs its layers four times per token, and Anthropic's HH-RLHF data, the answer is yes, but only faintly. A linear probe picks the preferred reply 61.5% of the time, a small nonlinear network that scores each reply separately 64.9%, and the evaluator trained for version 1 reaches 64.7% on the test split: clearly better than simple rules such as picking the longer reply, but weak. Whether preference is stored as a comparison between the two replies or as a property of each is still open. A linear probe cannot tell, and a network that reads both replies together has an estimated edge of only 0.7 points (95% CI 0.0 to 1.4) over one that scores each reply separately. These numbers hold under three controls: scoring every pair in both orders, splitting the data by pair, and, for the probes, keeping the end of each conversation, where the two replies differ. Version 1's 95.2% and 84.5% were obtained without the first two and do not hold; version 2's corrected relational-probe accuracy, obtained without the third, was four to five points too low. This version replaces both.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kirin

item.title: WorldComposer: Generative High-Fidelity Simulation with Digital Cousins for Generalizable Robot Learning and Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2604.15805v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning robust robot policies in real-world environments requires diverse data augmentation, yet scaling real-world data collection is costly due to the need for acquiring physical assets and reconfiguring environments. Therefore, augmenting real-world scenes into simulation has become a practical augmentation for efficient learning and evaluation. We present WorldComposer, an automated generative Real2Sim2Real framework that maps real-world panoramas into high-fidelity, task-ready simulation environments and further synthesizes diverse Digital Cousins through scene and object variations. Combined with high-quality physics engines and realistic assets, WorldComposer supports interactive manipulation across rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Additionally, we incorporate multi-room stitching to construct consistent large-scale environments for long-horizon tasks. Experiments demonstrate a strong sim-to-real correlation validating our platform's fidelity, and show that extensively scaling up data generation leads to significantly better generalization to unseen scene and object variations, demonstrating the effectiveness of Digital Cousins for generalizable robot learning and evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Jasper Lu, Zhenhao Shen, Yuanfei Wang, Shugao Liu, Shengqiang Xu, Shawn Xie, Jingkai Xu, Feng Jiang, Jade Yang, Chen Xie, Ruihai Wu

item.title: HorizonBench: Long-Horizon Personalization with Evolving Preferences
item.description: arXiv:2604.17283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Personal assistants now talk with the same user for months, and users' preferences change as their lives change; an assistant that keeps serving a preference the user has outgrown fails that user. Real conversations do not record when or why a preference changed, and existing benchmarks either hold preferences fixed or have the user state the change, so they cannot tell whether a model forgot what the user said or failed to update its belief about the user. We introduce HorizonBench and its data generator, which samples how a user's preferences change and generates six months of conversation from that sequence; each change follows a life event that the user mentions without stating the new preference. A human longitudinal preference dataset that we collect and release, 83,024 ratings from 160 people over 13 weeks, sets how often and how much life events change preferences. HorizonBench contains 4,245 questions from 360 users, and when a preference has changed, its earlier value is one of the answer options. All 25 frontier models we evaluate choose the outdated preference more often than evenly spread errors would predict, and the best reaches 52.8% accuracy. Two of the newest models score no higher when given only the relevant conversations than with the full history, yet one added sentence stating the change raises their accuracy by 11 to 22 points, and retrieval and memory methods do not recover the lost accuracy. Remembering what a user said and knowing what the user prefers now are therefore separate capabilities, and HorizonBench, its generator, and the human dataset support research on both.
item.dc:creator: Shuyue Stella Li, Bhargavi Paranjape, Kerem Oktar, Zhongyao Ma, Gelin Zhou, Lin Guan, Na Zhang, Sem Park, Lin Chen, Diyi Yang, Yulia Tsvetkov, Asli Celikyilmaz

item.title: MedExAgent: Training LLM Agents to Ask, Examine, and Diagnose in Noisy Clinical Environments
item.description: arXiv:2605.07058v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-world clinical diagnosis is a complex process in which the doctor is required to obtain information from both interaction with the patient and conducting medical exams. Additionally, the doctor needs to adapt to different patient personas, as well as noisy and incomplete information that can happen at any time during the process. However, existing benchmarks for medical LLMs and methods for automatic diagnosis largely simplify this process by reducing it to single-turn question answering, noise-free conversations, or sequential exam making, etc., ignoring the interactive and uncertain nature of clinical diagnosis. In this paper, we aim to address this gap by formalizing clinical diagnosis as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with three action types: questioning the patient, ordering medical exams as tool calls, and issuing a diagnosis. We also introduce a systematic noise model comprising seven patient noise types and three exam noise types. Using our proposed environment, we train an effective diagnosis agent, \textbf{MedExAgent}, through a two-stage pipeline that first performs supervised finetuning on synthetic conversations structured after the Calgary-Cambridge model for clinical interviews, and then applies DAPO to optimize a composite reward capturing diagnostic accuracy, tool call quality, and exam cost including financial cost and patient discomfort. Through extensive experiments and ablation studies, we demonstrate that MedExAgent achieves diagnostic performance comparable to larger models while maintaining cost-efficient examination strategies.
item.dc:creator: Yicheng Gao, Xiaolin Zhou, Yahan Li, Yue Zhao, Ruishan Liu

item.title: Learning to Decide with AI Assistance under Human-Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2605.12646v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: It is widely agreed that when AI models assist decision-makers in high-stakes domains by predicting an outcome of interest, they should communicate the confidence of their predictions. However, empirical evidence suggests that decision-makers often struggle to determine when to trust a prediction based solely on this communicated confidence. In this context, recent theoretical and empirical work suggests a positive correlation between the utility of AI-assisted decision-making and the degree of alignment between the AI confidence and the decision-makers' confidence in their own predictions. Crucially, these findings do not yet elucidate the extent to which this alignment influences the complexity of learning to make optimal decisions through repeated interactions. In this paper, we address this question in the canonical case of binary predictions and binary decisions. We first show that this problem is equivalent to a two-armed online contextual learning problem with full feedback, and establish a lower bound of $\Omega (\sqrt{|H| \cdot |B| \cdot T} )$ on the expected regret any learner can attain, where $H$ and $B$ denote the sets of human and AI confidence values. We then demonstrate that, under perfect alignment between AI and human confidence, a learner can attain an expected regret of $O(\sqrt{|H| \cdot T\log T})$ and, when $\sqrt{|H|} = O(\log T)$ and $B$ is countable, a non-trivial generalization of the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality improves the regret bound to $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$. Taken together, these results reveal that alignment can reduce the complexity of learning to make decisions with AI assistance. Experiments on real data from two different human-subject studies where participants solve simple decision-making tasks assisted by AI models show that our theoretical results are robust to violations of perfect alignment.
item.dc:creator: Nina Corvelo Benz, Eleni Straitouri, Manuel Gomez-Rodriguez

item.title: REALM: Retrospective Encoder Alignment for LFP Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2605.14867v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spike activity has been the dominant neural signal for behavior decoding because its high spatiotemporal resolution supports accurate decoding. However, as intracortical brain-computer interfaces (iBCIs) move toward higher channel counts and wireless operation, the high sampling rates required to record spikes create substantial power and bandwidth demands. Local field potentials (LFPs) offer complementary advantages, including greater long-term stability, lower energy consumption, and lower bandwidth requirements. However, LFP-based decoders often achieve lower accuracy and rely on non-causal architectures that cannot be used directly for real-time deployment. We propose REALM, a retrospective knowledge distillation (RKD) framework for causal LFP behavior decoding. Inspired by offline-to-online distillation in speech recognition, REALM transfers non-causal representational knowledge from a pretrained, multi-session bidirectional LFP teacher to a causal student model. We first pretrain a bidirectional Mamba-2 teacher across multiple recording sessions using continuous masked autoencoding (CMAE), and then distill its representation into a compact causal student using a combined objective of representation alignment and autoencoding. REALM achieves the highest mean accuracy among the compared decoders in both label-free and fine-tuned pipelines, with statistically significant improvements over each baseline, including the state-of-the-art CrossModalDistill. It does so using LFPs alone throughout pretraining, distillation, and decoding, with less than half the parameters of CrossModalDistill's published student and one-tenth of its pretraining time. These results show that a causal LFP-only model can achieve decoding accuracy competitive with a non-causal multi-modal model, offering a practical and scalable approach for next-generation wireless and implantable iBCIs.
item.dc:creator: Peicheng Wu, Zhenyu Bu, Runze Ma, Lin Du

item.title: What competing constraints reveal about representation learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.15995v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning latent states from temporal, multimodal, and partially observed data requires decisions about what information representations should retain, discard, and organize. I argue that six complementary properties help clarify these decisions: predictive sufficiency, minimality, temporal coherence, observation compatibility, nuisance invariance, and structural constraints. Drawing on established approaches, I distinguish desired representation properties from the objectives used to encourage them and the diagnostics used to assess them, since neither a training objective nor an evaluation metric guarantees that a property has been achieved. Controlled synthetic experiments examine how training objectives influence predictive performance, nuisance decodability, and latent organization. The results reveal discrepancies between seemingly favorable diagnostics and the information retained in learned representations, as well as latent-coordinate ambiguities under equivalent predictive performance, illustrating how complementary evaluations can improve interpretation and guide design choices. Together, these analyses provide a basis for designing, comparing, and evaluating learned latent states.
item.dc:creator: Gwenol\'e Quellec

item.title: KVBuffer: IO-aware Serving for Linear Attention
item.description: arXiv:2605.19049v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Linear attention has recently gained significant attention for long-context inference due to its constant decoding cost with respect to context length. However, existing serving systems typically serve linear attention by recurrently computing and updating a large linear attention state in every decoding step. Since the state is much larger than the per-token key and value, recurrent decoding incurs substantial memory access and becomes inefficient for serving linear attention. In this paper, we propose KVBuffer, an IO-aware serving mechanism for linear attention. By buffering recent keys and values, KVBuffer enables serving systems to compute linear attention outputs in more flexible and memory-efficient ways. For decoding, KVBuffer enables chunkwise computation, which reduces average memory access and decoding latency by deferring state updates and applying them in batch. For speculative decoding, KVBuffer verifies draft tokens in parallel and avoids storing temporary states. For short contexts, KVBuffer computes attention outputs directly from buffered keys and values, without creating or updating the linear attention state. We implement KVBuffer in SGLang for Qwen3.5 and Nemotron-3 series models. Our evaluations show that KVBuffer can speedup batch decoding by up to 1.47x and increase the maximum number of serving requests by 5x for speculative decoding when verifying four draft tokens.
item.dc:creator: Longwei Zou, Lin Zhong

item.title: Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Language Models via Infilling
item.description: arXiv:2605.24173v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Memorization in large language models has been studied almost exclusively through prefix-conditioned extraction, a natural choice for autoregressive models. However, diffusion language models (DLMs) can denoise masked tokens at arbitrary positions. Thus, prefix-only probing reveals only one facet of memorization in DLMs and significantly underestimates the risk of training-data extraction. In order to realistically model extractability of training data in DLMs, we introduce infilling extraction, a data-extraction protocol parameterized by an arbitrary binary mask that subsumes prefix-only probing and accounts for the bidirectional inductive bias of DLMs. Instantiating it on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across five extraction modes, three training pipelines, and three corpora covering verbatim and partial leakage, we find that mask geometry governs extractability: edge-conditioned masks extract up to three times more verbatim sequences than prefix-conditioned ones, and bidirectional access opens channels inaccessible in autoregressive models. In particular, an adversary who obtains a PII-redacted copy of the training data can use targeted infilling to raise PII recall on fine-tuned DLMs by 2.5-4.5x over prefix-conditioned extraction, substantially narrowing the gap to a scale-matched autoregressive model and, for LLaDA on email addresses, exceeding it under greedy prefix-conditioned extraction. Tunable parameters for decoding measurably affect extraction performance, while a follow-up supervised fine-tuning stage does not eliminate the prior memorization.
item.dc:creator: Yihan Wang, N. Asokan

item.title: LLM-Assisted Reranking to Operationalize Nuanced Objectives in Recommender Systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.02883v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recommender systems shape what information we see, raising concerns about filter bubbles, radicalization, polarization, and social inequality. Large language models (LLMs) enable more powerful personalization that may intensify these dynamics, yet most recommenders are tuned for engagement or narrow accuracy metrics, with little attention to broader social effects. We investigate whether LLM-assisted reranking, while improving personalization, inadvertently amplifies exposure to ideologically congenial, extreme, or conspiratorial political content, a risk theorized but not yet empirically characterized. Using real YouTube trajectories, we rerank the platform's sidebar candidates by zero-shot prompting across three models, alongside an embedding baseline, and evaluate relevance, ideological alignment and diversity, and exposure to conspiratorial or extremist content. We find that (i) under a pure personalization instruction, reranking improves relevance while narrowing ideological exposure and, on two of three models, promoting problematic content for users with such histories; the third model, which declines most explicitly partisan requests, points to model-specific guardrails; (ii) lightweight prompt-level constraints substantially reduce problematic exposure on all three models, while the regularized rerankers still rank above the platform baseline on relevance; and (iii) synthetic experiments varying topical and partisan cues independently show no fixed preference between them: topic dominates on abortion and immigration, while partisanship takes over on elections, where the topical signal is weaker. Our results highlight the power of LLMs to operationalize contextual nuance in high-stakes political recommendation, and underscore the need to evaluate LLM-assisted personalization beyond accuracy and to treat prompt design as a value-laden choice rather than a neutral default.
item.dc:creator: Amir Ghasemian, Homa Hosseinmardi, Upasana Dutta, Duncan J. Watts

item.title: Measuring What Matters: Synthetic Benchmarks for Concept Bottleneck Models
item.description: arXiv:2606.04326v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Concept bottleneck models predict using high-level concepts detected in inputs. Although these models provide a simple way to reap benefits from interpretability, they are hard to train and evaluate because very few real-world datasets include concept labels. In this paper, we develop synthetic benchmarks for concept bottleneck models. With our benchmarks, researchers can generate labeled datasets and control properties that affect performance, such as data modality, the choice of concepts, or annotation quality. They can thus find problems that suit these models and isolate the factors behind their failures. We demonstrate how our benchmarks can be used to evaluate major use cases for concept bottleneck models: decision support, i.e., helping human experts make better decisions; and automation, i.e., handling routine tasks without supervision. Our demonstrations show how the benchmarks can identify new failure modes and attribute them to either the architecture or the data.
item.dc:creator: Julian Skirzynski, Harry Cheon, Shreyas Kadekodi, Meredith Stewart, Berk Ustun

item.title: Accounting for Purchased Artificial Intelligence Inference in Corporate Greenhouse Gas Inventories: A Token-Based Method
item.description: arXiv:2606.10660v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Purchased artificial intelligence (AI) inference belongs in Scope 3 Category 1 of a corporate greenhouse gas inventory, yet practice omits it or applies a spend-based factor that gives 1.7 to 12.3 times the physical estimate and cannot tell one model or region from another. This paper sets out a token-based method and open dataset: a cradle-to-gate boundary, four tiers of activity data, an effective-token basis, a four-term factor (serving electricity, embodied hardware, data-centre construction, disclosed final training runs) and a rule resolving any model identifier and region to a factor. Inference footprints span twelve times between model classes and nine between regions. The mid-class factor, 0.039 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per million billed tokens at the world-average grid, is the low end of a stated structural range: a less efficient serving configuration raises it 2.8 times, and replacing the training term with all model development, on its own boundary, gives 1.5 to 2.9 times it. Input bands alone give -18% to +29%. Published per-query energy estimates that can describe a mid-class model are 2.4 to 7.2 times the mid-class energy, above its structural range in four of five rows; those that can describe a frontier-class model bracket it at 0.7 to 1.6 times. Worked examples give 8.5 kg CO2e a year for a 200-person firm, and 2.1 tonnes for fifty developers using agentic coding tools on a mid-class model or 8.3 tonnes on a frontier-class one. The contribution is a traceable figure; accuracy against metered energy is untested.
item.dc:creator: Guillermo Llopis-Garcia (SOMA AI, Barcelona)

item.title: Rational Sparse Autoencoder
item.description: arXiv:2606.14990v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are standard tools for mechanistic interpretability, but current SAE families are constrained by fixed encoder nonlinearities such as ReLU, JumpReLU, and TopK. This hard-codes a particular sparsity mechanism into the model and can distort the reconstruction-versus-sparsity trade-off. We introduce the Rational Sparse Autoencoder (RSAE), which replaces the fixed encoder activation with a trainable rational function. The design is motivated by a reconstruction advantage that we prove for RSAE at matched expected sparsity, with guaranteed non-inferiority to ReLU and, under stated assumptions, provable improvements over JumpReLU and TopK. The model is then implemented through a two-stage pipeline: an initialization procedure that copies the pre-trained baseline SAE weights and calibrates the scale parameters along with the rational coefficients; followed by a fine-tuning step under a sparsity-regularized reconstruction objective that holds $\ell_0$ at the teacher's value. Consistent with this theory, on residual-stream activations of three open-weight language models and across all three baseline activation families, the RSAE improves reconstruction fidelity after the fine-tuning step at the same level of sparsity. These gains are consistent across host language models, across baseline activation families, and across the full range of baseline sparsity we tested, while the upgrade itself adds only 20 scalar parameters per autoencoder and one training run takes between about 4 and 25 minutes on a single consumer GPU.
item.dc:creator: Naiyu Yin, Maosen Tang, Alex Townsend, Yue Yu

item.title: Robustness of Text-Only Adapted Speech LLMs for Spoken Semantic Parsing
item.description: arXiv:2606.21453v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate structured outputs from natural language instructions, including semantic frames and function calls. When the input is speech, this task becomes spoken semantic parsing, which can be performed using either Speech LLMs or ASR-LLM cascades. Although both approaches can be adapted with text-only task supervision, their relative robustness to acoustic degradation remains unclear. We compare these approaches under matched text-form supervision using 3B and 7B models across three datasets, evaluated on clean speech and babble noise at five SNR levels. Results show that Speech LLMs generally achieve better performance in command understanding, intent prediction, and function calling, particularly under severe noise, while improvements in fine-grained entity prediction are less consistent. An additional evaluation shows that Speech LLMs achieve lower average inference time per sample than ASR-LLM cascades at both model scales.
item.dc:creator: Youngwon Choi, Donghyuk Jung, Hyeonyu Kim, Taeyoun Kwon, Myeongkyun Cho, Moon Hwan Kim

item.title: Multi-Modal Environment-Aware Beam Management for Massive MIMO: A Geometry-Driven Virtual Base Station Framework
item.description: arXiv:2606.26567v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-frequency massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems promise ultra-high data rates. However, efficient beam management remains challenging due to the prohibitive beam training overhead and intricate coordination required in multi-user MIMO (MU-MIMO) scenarios. To address these bottlenecks, environment-aware communications have emerged as a promising paradigm, leveraging site-specific knowledge to circumvent exhaustive pilot-based beam training and streamline multi-user communications. In this paper, we propose a geometry-driven framework that utilizes multi-modal environmental data, specifically regional 3D light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds and location information, to construct an offline virtual base station (VBS) database. By modeling dominant reflection paths via mirror symmetry across building facades reconstructed from the point clouds, the VBS database provides a compact and sparse description of the wireless propagation environment. Given a user location, the VBS representation supports online coarse channel reconstruction and the generation of a beamspace prior. To refine the coarse estimates, we design a VBS-assisted orthogonal-pilot (VOP)-based partial beam training scheme with limited online measurements. Finally, to coordinate beam selection under inter-user interference, we develop a hierarchical dual-agent dueling double deep Q-network for coordinated beam selection (DD3QN-CBS). Simulation results show that the proposed framework improves effective spectral efficiency over the evaluated stochastic, heuristic, and conventional learning-based baselines, while achieving competitive performance with fewer online beam measurements.
item.dc:creator: Yijie Bian, Wei Guo, Jie Yang, Shenghui Song, Jun Zhang, Shi Jin, Khaled B. Letaief

item.title: SharQ: Bridging Activation Sparsity and FP4 Quantization for LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2606.26587v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Low-bit floating-point formats and semi-structured sparsity are increasingly supported by modern accelerators, yet combining them for LLM activation compression remains challenging: activations contain input-dependent outliers that dominate block scales in FP4 quantization, and directly applying N:M sparsity masks discards moderate values, coupling sparsification loss with quantization error. We introduce SharQ, a training-free inference method that bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization through an online sparse--dense decomposition. For each activation tensor, SharQ generates an input-adaptive N:M mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes it to FP4, and defines a dense residual relative to the quantized sparse backbone rather than the unquantized sparse values. A sparse FP4 GEMM processes the backbone while a dense FP4 GEMM compensates for both mask-induced activation loss and sparse-path quantization error. The two paths share a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views, and a fused preparation kernel absorbs mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one operator. SharQ requires no calibration data, retraining, or model-specific tuning. Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43--63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks, and generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats. On an RTX 5090, SharQ delivers 2.2--2.4$\times$ latency reduction over FP16 and 1.2--1.4$\times$ throughput improvement over FP8 in language model serving, and up to 1.58$\times$ speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation when combined with SageAttention. Our code is available at https://github.com/actypedef/SharQ.
item.dc:creator: Haoqian Meng, Yilun Luo, Yafei Zhao, Wenyuan Liu, Huaqing Zheng, Xindian Ma, Peng Zhang

item.title: Brownian Bridge Diffusion-Assisted Joint Channel Estimation and Data Detection for Jamming-Resilient OFDM Receivers
item.description: arXiv:2606.28778v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In next-generation wireless networks, the growing density of devices and limited spectrum resources pose severe jamming challenges to fragile legitimate communication links in the wireless electromagnetic environment. Crucially, when jamming overlaps with pilot and data symbols in both time and frequency domains, it inflicts a severe bottleneck on receiver-side joint estimation and detection. Existing schemes often lack an effective framework to combat such jamming contamination, thereby failing to guarantee reliable transmission. To address this issue, we propose a Brownian bridge diffusion-assisted joint channel estimation and data detection (BBD-JCED) framework for jamming-resilient orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) receivers. The proposed framework consists of a jamming suppression module and a Brownian bridge-joint recovery module. The former identifies jamming-contaminated bins in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain and suppresses the dominant jamming components through spectral notching. The latter establishes a Brownian bridge-based probabilistic graph to model the probabilistic transition process from the suppressed OFDM observation to the coded bits, and performs a reverse recovery process to enable enhanced joint channel estimation and data detection. Moreover, we derive a variational lower bound (VLB) to reformulate the intractable bit estimate problem into a tractable training objective, providing a probabilistic foundation for the loss function design. Furthermore, we develop a two-stage training algorithm to separately optimize the jamming suppression and Brownian bridge-joint recovery modules. Simulation results under representative jamming types demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior jamming suppression and bit recovery performance over the considered baseline schemes while maintaining competitive inference complexity.
item.dc:creator: Honghan She, Yufan Cheng, Siya Huang, Pengyu Wang, Tieming Sun, Kaikai Yang

item.title: A Geometric Coding Theorem
item.description: arXiv:2607.13796v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper establishes a direct analogue of the classical Coding Theorem in the setting of symmetry groups. We consider computable bijections on the set of binary strings and define the symmetry prior of a string x as the probability that a randomly chosen symmetry from a given group G has x as its unique fixed point. We show that for any fix-retractable symmetry group G, a group admitting a computable section that selects an isolating symmetry for every string, the symmetry prior is a universal lower semi-computable semi-measure. In this case, the Geometric Coding Theorem holds. This result is a coding-theoretic restatement of a theorem of Trejo, Kreinovich and Longpr\'e, who showed that the complexity of describing a string by a symmetry with that string as its unique fixed point equals its Kolmogorov complexity. Our contribution is to recast it in terms of algorithmic probability and to treat the symmetry group as a parameter, identifying fix-retractability as exactly the condition under which symmetry complexity collapses onto Kolmogorov complexity.
item.dc:creator: Romie Banerjee

item.title: Operational Proto-Introspection in Looped Language Models: Reading Correctness Before the Answer
item.description: arXiv:2607.18553v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can one tell, while a language model reasons, whether its answer will be right? Looped models are a good place to ask: they run the same layers several times per token, leaving one hidden state per loop for a probe to read. I probe Ouro-RLTT, a 2.6B-parameter looped model, for what these states reveal about how its reasoning will end. I call such information operational proto-introspection: operational because it is defined by what a probe can read, and proto because nothing here shows that the model itself uses it. In part, yes. Reading the first 48 tokens of reasoning, from answers that state no answer yet, a probe on the hidden states reaches an AUROC of 0.758 on a synthetic logic task, against 0.515 for token confidence. Question difficulty is a rival explanation: on 1,164 further questions, token confidence plus simple features of the question predict about as well. It is not only difficulty: between two answers to the same question, the probe scores the correct one higher 74% of the time. A fine-tuned language model reading the same tokens does about as well. On GSM8K and on a second checkpoint this within-question test is unresolved. A probe that ranks finished candidate answers is weak at layer 8 on the first loop, much better on the second, and as accurate as the last layers by the third, on four Ouro checkpoints. The direction it reads is largely shared across loops: a probe trained on the last loop reads the first nearly as well as a probe trained there. The signal helps decide what to do with finished outputs. It improves abstention over surface features and picks correct answers among candidates better than chance, though surface features pick about as well. Once several samples are finished, a baseline that knows their agreement leaves the answer-free probe nothing measurable to add. None of my attempts to use it to make the model generate better answers worked.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kirin

item.title: Where Is the Cost of Third-Party API Routers in Agentic Software Development?
item.description: arXiv:2607.23624v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Third-party API routers have become a common layer that unifies access across increasingly diverse LLM providers. In coding-agent workflows, high-autonomy operation is widely adopted because it reduces interaction overhead. As a result, a third-party API router, which sits between the agent and the upstream provider, inevitably occupies the trusted path. It can inspect and modify every request and response, yet no mechanism verifies alignment between the provider's output and the repository-level actions ultimately executed by the agent. Consequently, client-side permission mechanisms may become ineffective in practice. Whether this control gap produces real, hard-to-detect effects on software development tasks remains empirically unmeasured. In this paper, we conduct an empirical study of router-side injection in coding agents, examining four intervention levels of increasing subtlety: Response Substitution (L1), Response Append (L2), LLM-Polished Injection (L3), and LLM-Polished with Distribution Alignment Injection (L4). Moreover, we develop SIDEL, a framework for trace recording, replay, injection, and defense evaluation, with a curated dataset of 400 samples. We evaluate four representative coding agents, and further evaluate whitelist-based execution control and LLM review. Router-side intervention substantially alters repository-level actions and remains difficult for existing client-side safeguards to detect. Without additional mitigations, all evaluated agents achieved a defense success rate of 0 percent across all injection levels. Client-side mitigations and reactive reviews improve resistance but do not fully restore end-to-end control, motivating provider-side output-integrity guarantees. Our code is available at https://github.com/Riyasushin/SIDEL.
item.dc:creator: Donghao Fu, Jingxin Li, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong

item.title: SciFigQual-Bench: Scientific Figure Quality Assessment with Manuscript-Linked Context
item.description: arXiv:2607.27084v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scientific figure quality is bound to the manuscript: a crop can be visually clear and still contradict its caption or the paragraph that cites it. Most image quality assessment and chart-understanding methods target a detached visual surface or a question-answering score, rather than alignment among the figure, its caption, and the citing text. A single end-to-end prompt that sees the image and the text together still mixes what is visible with what the caption and the citing paragraph claim, so fluent wording can raise a visual score and missing text can be treated as low quality. To address this gap, we introduce SciFigQual-Bench, a manuscript-linked benchmark for published CS-conference figures that binds each figure to its caption and to index-resolved citing paragraphs, and scores visual clarity, layout, caption consistency, context consistency, and misleading risk, leaving a dimension unevaluated when its evidence is absent. SFQ-Agent reads the image and the text in separate calls and records modality-specific evidence. A cross-modal judge scores caption and citing-text alignment from those reports, and a deterministic runner keeps the visual scores, sets misleading risk by a fixed rule, and applies the written caps, so each dimension follows the rubric instead of a single end-to-end prompt. Experiments comparing this staged judge with single-pass and OCR-sidecar protocols find the closest point-estimate fit to mean human ratings under staged judging, while the gap between protocols remains small. Caption consistency remains the main gap, and agreement with the rater mean answers a different question from agreement among human raters. Project page: https://frankdengai.github.io/SciFigQual-Bench/
item.dc:creator: Zihan Deng, Chuanzhi Xu, Huiqi Liang, Xiaozhen Zhong, Weidong Cai, Lequan Yu

item.title: MANGO-Grasp: Mahalanobis Fields over Geometry-Oriented 3D Gaussians for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping
item.description: arXiv:2608.02014v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasping aims to synthesize stable grasps across heterogeneous multi-fingered hands with little or no embodiment-specific tuning. Existing interaction-centric methods achieve promising results, but their object representations often underrepresent local surface geometry, hand descriptors do not explicitly capture both morphology and kinematics, and hand-object interaction modeling is typically isotropic. We propose MANGO-Grasp, an anisotropic interaction framework that represents objects as geometry-oriented 3D Gaussian primitives to better preserve local surface geometry, and encodes hands into pretrained descriptors that capture both morphology and kinematics. Hand-object interaction is modeled using anisotropic Mahalanobis fields that reflect the directional nature of contact and guide a shared optimization for grasp realization across embodiments. On the CMAP and MultiGripperGrasp benchmarks, MANGO-Grasp outperforms the strongest seen-hand baseline by up to 8.24 percentage points in simulation. It also transfers zero-shot to the unseen SharpaWave hand, improving over the strongest zero-shot baseline by up to 16.57 percentage points, and achieves 86% success in real-world experiments. The code and additional materials are available at https://connor-zh.github.io/MANGO-Grasp/.
item.dc:creator: Heng Zhang, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Mike Zheng Shou, Weisi Lin, Yan Wu

item.title: Scrouting: Cost-Aware Routing of Coding Agents by Scouting the Repository First
item.description: arXiv:2608.04804v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frontier language models can resolve repository-level software issues, but each attempt is expensive, and existing routers select a model from the issue text alone. We present SuperScout, which routes after scouting the repository: a 7B searcher, SuperScout-7B, first explores the repository and produces a structured handoff whose reproduction claims are sandbox-verified, with false claims stripped before delivery. The searcher's hidden states, together with the task text, then feed a resume-based router that dispatches the task to one of four frontier fixers. Adding a new fixer requires no retraining. On the full Python slice of SWE-bench Pro (266 tasks) under the benchmark's official capped budget tier, SuperScout matches the best single model's solve rate (159 of 266 for SuperScout, 158 for the best model) at about a fifth of the total cost per solve, and the reported configuration sits above the random traffic-splitting baseline. A no-router ablation, always the cheapest fixer with the handoff, ties the routed system on this benchmark, so the handoff rather than the routing decision carries the result. A paired calibration study points to the mechanism: the handoff appears to redistribute rather than add solving ability, lifting the three cheaper fixers while slightly hurting the strongest, though at $N=99$ the per-fixer effects are directional only; the searcher's hidden states improve cost routing on the calibration labels while the handoff's own text does not. The searcher's compute adds less than half a cent of GPU time per task.
item.dc:creator: Ishaan Bhola, Adithyan Krishnan, Mukunda NS, Dhruv Jaglan

item.title: How do features act in an individual prediction? Separating standalone and interaction effects with a case-based taxonomy
item.description: arXiv:2608.27821v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Local explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME summarize each feature with a single attribution score, and interaction indices quantify how strongly features interact. Neither tells a user how a feature acts in a given prediction: whether its effect is the same alone and in context, or whether the other features amplify it, make it unnecessary, switch it off or reverse it. We extend case-based feature importance (CBFI), originally a global method, to individual predictions. Evaluating the model in four hybrid states per background sample decomposes the in-context importance of a feature into a standalone and an interaction effect, and a case taxonomy labels each feature of an instance as inactive, standalone, amplified, redundant, gated or reversed. We compare the method with k-SII, TreeSHAP interaction values and the H-statistic on synthetic functions, and study eight real tabular datasets with six model families. On the true functions, the decomposition recovered interactions exactly (correlation 0.99 with the analytic local interaction). On fitted models, pair recovery was slightly below that of dedicated indices (local precision@k 0.86-0.91 versus 0.91-0.95). Interaction values alone could not distinguish substitution from gating, whereas the taxonomy identified both without knowing the partner (accuracy 0.74-0.76); applied to Shapley interaction values, it performed comparably. On real data, 45-57% of feature pairs with nearly identical SHAP values received different labels, and in a medical-insurance model the method showed that the interaction component of smoking changes sign at a body-mass index of 30. Localized CBFI does not detect interactions more accurately than existing indices; what it adds is a decomposition into standalone and interaction effects and a label stating how each feature acts.
item.dc:creator: Sejong Oh

item.title: Autonomous discovery of new structure-plausibility laws for explainable and rapid crystal diagnosis and screening
item.description: arXiv:2609.01209v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative models and autonomous agents now propose candidate inorganic crystals by the million, yet most screens test little beyond a minimum-distance cutoff and give no chemical reason for failure. For nearly a century, Pauling's rules have served as the main empirical theory of crystal-structure stability, but they remain qualitative and idealized, leading to only 6.5% of known ionic crystals satisfying rules 2--5 simultaneously. Here our agents generate, test and refute two million candidate laws to discover eight Plausibility Rules for Inorganic Structures (PRIS). These laws encode five physical mechanisms: short-range repulsion, ionic contact and packing, electrostatic balance, bond-valence conservation and crystallographic site simplicity. Experimental structures satisfy the PRIS law sets in 82--99% of cases, and the strictest set detects 87.9% of artificially damaged structures, far above the 1.6--3.2% of conventional distance cutoffs. Although derived without synthesis labels, PRIS plausibility is highly linearly correlated with synthesizability, and a continuous PRIS-derived synthesis score (PSS) explainably filters out 83.7% of hard-to-synthesize structures while retaining 80.7% of experimental structures. In an inverse-design task targeting ultra-incompressible crystals, explainable screening by PRIS and PSS cuts the density functional theory (DFT) validation queue by up to 67.3% while retaining 99.2% of the DFT-verified target candidates. Beyond screening, PRIS traces GNoME's low-symmetry excess to artificial element ordering and identifies falsified crystal structures. PRIS moves screening from a pass-or-fail verdict to a chemical reason for failure, showing that autonomous agents can discover, by active refutation, physicochemical laws that guide calculations and experiments.
item.dc:creator: Zhilong Song, Heung Law, Lixue Cheng

item.title: OracleZoom: Reference-Constrained Recursive Image Super-Resolution Beyond Ground Truth
