item.description: arXiv:2609.06490v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recursive image Super-Resolution (SR) reaches extreme magnification by feeding each prediction back into the same model, like zooming into an image again and again. Real ground truth for deep zooms is impractical to capture (a full $256\times$ target would be a 52 GB image), so predictions at deeper zooms have no supervision. Yet the last ground-truth image still contains the region that every deeper zoom magnifies. OracleZoom turns this region into a training signal. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation, the model trains on its own prediction for one recursive step ($4\times \rightarrow 16\times$), and a cross-scale loss projects each $16\times$ prediction back to the last ground truth at $4\times$. This projection can verify only coarse content, so a no-reference quality objective guides the remaining fine detail, and a latent prior stops this objective from adding hallucinated artifacts. On seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves the highest CLIPIQA at every zoom depth (mean 0.713 vs. 0.621 for Chain-of-Zoom), with the largest gains at the deepest zooms, even though training stops at $16\times$ and optimizes a different quality metric. Pooled over two ground-truth-anchored judges, this added detail comes at the same hallucination rate as Chain-of-Zoom at $16\times$ and a lower rate at $4\times$, and removing the cross-scale loss raises hallucination at $16\times$.
item.dc:creator: Shubhashis Roy Dipta, Nobin Sarwar, Md Rizwan Parvez

item.title: TabBench-Bio: A Living Benchmark for Machine Learning on High-Dimensional Biomedical Tables
item.description: arXiv:2609.07441v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Biomedical tables often combine thousands of measured variables with only tens or hundreds of labelled samples, a regime that is poorly represented in general-purpose tabular benchmarks. We introduce TabBench-Bio, a living and interactive benchmark of 43 biomedical datasets spanning multiple domains. Under a shared cross-validation protocol, we compare classical estimators, neural networks, and tabular foundation models across 28 feature-by-sample operating points. At the reference cell of 10,000 features and 100 training samples, RealTabPFN 2.5 has the highest point estimate, closely followed by TabPFN 3 and Logistic Regression. A paired bootstrap over the target pool separates RealTabPFN 2.5 from TabPFN 3 by 87 Elo (95\% interval [43, 129]). Tabular foundation models generally occupy the leading ranks, while the strongest configuration depends on the operating point and biomedical modality. The AutoML framework AutoGluon, using its one-hour "extreme" preset, is configured as a separate resource-intensive reference and reported here at the reference and full cell. Fold-level predictions, run status, and deterministic aggregations make every reported result reproducible and reusable. The benchmark is open to contributions of new biomedical datasets. The interactive leaderboard is available at https://tabbench-bio.eu.
item.dc:creator: Jules Kreuer, Sofiane Ouaari, Julia Hellmig, Julius Braitinger, Nico Pfeifer

item.title: Improving Cross-Lingual Token Representations by Adding a Pinch of SALT
item.description: arXiv:2609.09953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cross-lingual sentence encoders enable scalable transfer across hundreds of languages, powering applications such as translation mining and zero-shot learning in low-resource settings. Although trained for sentence-level alignment, they are increasingly also applied to token-level tasks such as hallucination detection and sequence tagging, exposing a mismatch between training and usage. We propose SALT, a lightweight post-training method that improves token representations by injecting span-level supervision into existing sentence encoders. Across five multilingual token-level benchmarks, SALT achieves the best overall results on four of them, outperforming alternative fine-tuning strategies and competitive encoders. It also improves sentence-level performance on cross-lingual retrieval and classification tasks. These results demonstrate that span-level supervision is an effective signal for improving both token and sentence representations.
item.dc:creator: Guillem Ram\'irez

item.title: RPMem: Learning Long-Term Recurrent Parametric Memory Across Sessions for LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.23466v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-running LLM agents require memory that persists and evolves across sessions. Text-based memory retrieves and reconstructs past interactions at every query, making long-horizon performance increasingly dependent on retrieval quality and contextual reasoning as histories grow. Parametric memory encodes experience directly into model computation, but existing approaches provide limited support for cross-session memory evolution. Their coupling to a specific backbone further restricts memory reuse after model replacement. We introduce RPMem, a two-stage architecture that compiles each session into a model-independent latent memory through forward computation and selectively integrates it with retained memory via a task-trained recurrent gate. The consolidated memory is then mapped to backbone-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) parameters, allowing the encoding capability to transfer when the backbone is replaced. Evaluation across three long-term memory benchmarks and five diverse backbones demonstrates broad generalization with near-constant update cost and memory footprint. With Qwen3-8B on PERMA, RPMem reaches 85.52%, outperforming the strongest parametric and text-based baselines by 5.32 and 12.98 percentage points, respectively. Ablations validate the complementary roles of session compilation and cross-session consolidation, while dynamics analyses reveal that the gate acquires task-specific memory integration strategies. These results establish RPMem as a lifecycle-independent parametric memory framework that maintains evolving cross-session memory that remains reusable across backbone replacements. Our code is available at https://github.com/Quark-Medical/rpmem/tree/main.
item.dc:creator: Fanyu Zhao, Ruike Cao, Liang Dong, Fugen Yao, Jian Xu, Guanjun Jiang, Yinsheng Li, Yifei Zhao, Han Zhang

item.title: When Does Reallocating a Sampling Budget Pay? Instance-wise Allocation for Neural Routing Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2609.27917v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural routing solvers sample many solutions per instance and keep the best, with the same number of samples for every instance. We measure how much a non-uniform split of the same total budget is worth and which property of a workload decides it. Best-of-k curves estimated by averaging random orderings of stored samples overstate the gain, and deciding on one half of the samples while evaluating on the other understates it; we use exact best-of-k curves, a U-statistic over all orderings. For three pretrained solvers (POMO, the Attention Model and Sym-NCO) on the traveling salesman problem, reallocation reduces the total optimality gap by at most 2.5% on the training distribution, so uniform allocation is close to optimal there. On workloads that mix in out-of-distribution instances it reduces the gap by 11.8-13.3% (1.1-1.8% of tour length) for the two solvers that degrade under the shift, and almost nothing for the one that does not. Across two heterogeneity mechanisms, three solvers, two confirmation collections and budgets of 25 to 200 samples per instance, the gain is predicted by the spread of difficulty within a workload, not its average. Allocating on a power-law curve fitted to twenty charged probe samples per instance recovers 88-93% of the uncharged optimum; successive halving does worse. A 2-opt local search, however, removes most of the gap at negligible cost, after which reallocation adds a few hundredths of a percent of tour length.
item.dc:creator: Jinhyung Bae

item.title: Who Is Behind the Harness? Verifying Model Identity in Coding Agents through Behavioral Fingerprinting
item.description: arXiv:2609.28559v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLMs increasingly operate through coding-agent harnesses that inspect repositories, invoke tools, and modify files. Substituting the model behind such an agent can therefore change security-relevant decisions, including whether it verifies changes or recovers safely from failures. Existing LLM fingerprints largely infer identity from direct text or token distributions. In coding agents, these signals are mediated by system instructions, controller logic, tools, and execution feedback, limiting their transfer. We present LIDAR (LLM Identification from Decisions and Actions at Runtime), an active black-box fingerprinting method for coding-agent execution. Three coding probe pairs expose post-edit verification, transient-failure recovery, and specification--test conflict resolution under controlled changes. LIDAR represents the resulting trajectories with complementary instance-level and distribution-level features and compares them with clean references using a lightweight probabilistic identifier. It requires no access to model weights, logits, or provider internals. We evaluate 24 models from eight families on OpenCode, OpenHands, and mini-swe-agent, fitting separate references for each harness. Closed-set Top-1 accuracy ranges from 91.39\% to 98.89\% across the three harnesses, exceeding all three baselines in each setting. When the audit also includes unregistered models from the same families, balanced accuracy ranges from 79.58\% to 80.42\%. These results show that agent execution behavior provides model-identity evidence beyond final outputs.
item.dc:creator: Chuyi Wang, Xiaohui Xie, Tongze Wang, Fangchen Luo, Yong Cui

item.title: Hearsay: Who Can Audit the Record a Deployed Agent Harness Writes?
item.description: arXiv:2609.32495v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The record of an agent's run is written by the harness that drives the agent. When the run is later disputed, the auditor was not there and has only this record. We ask whether someone who was not there can check the record, and what decides the answer. It depends on who wrote what a check can rely on: if the harness wrote all of it, the record is only the harness's own word, and we call it hearsay. We build Hearsay, a benchmark that examines the record and not the task: five harnesses run fourteen tasks, model examiners from three vendors and a human panel read the records and answer questions about the runs, and every passage they cite is labelled mechanically by who wrote it. We also audit what is deployed: in all sixteen frameworks, the harness is the only writer. With one writer, readers can name the fault from the record, in up to nine runs in ten, but they cannot check the record. The model examiners claim corroboration for 18 to 55 points more of their evidence than the labels support, a gap we then predicted for runs driven by another vendor's model and found again. And the best of them notices only half of the alterations we make to a record, while the two that name the fault most often cannot tell what a harness left out. With a second writer, the record can be checked. Our sandbox keeps a ledger of what passes between harness and model, and reading the ledger against the record in both directions shows what the record leaves out and what it adds. We test this as an auditor would use it, on one unseen record at a time. On runs driven by a third vendor's model, with every rule committed before the records existed, it reports 64 of 66 alterations and flags none of 84 clean records. On held-out records in five formats it reports 109 of 115. What makes a record evidence is a second writer, not a better reader.
item.dc:creator: Jiahong Dai, Zhuochen Yang, Pengyang Shao, Kelvin Ng, Zhongyi Liu, Chengquan Ju, Yuting He, Bo Hu

item.title: Orbits as Strong Models: Kolmogorov Structure Function under Symmetry
item.description: arXiv:2609.40290v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Strong models in algorithmic statistics are essentially the cells of simple partitions of $\{0,1\}^n$. We study the partitions that come from symmetry, the orbit partitions of groups acting on strings, and the structure function $h^G_x$ they induce. A set is a cell of such a partition exactly when its setwise stabiliser acts transitively on it, so $h^G_x$ is Kolmogorov's structure function restricted to $G$-homogeneous sets. For the full symmetric group this recovers all models and exactly the strong ones. For $GL(n,2)$ the cells are the linearly homogeneous sets, $h^{GL}_x$ lies in a band between $C(x)-\alpha$ and $n-\alpha$ with both edges attained, and some stochastic normal strings have simple structure that is invisible to linear symmetry. Writing each permutation group as a Burnside-ring type with a placement, we show that any space of symmetry hypotheses small enough to search is small enough to miss simple structure. Finally we cast the search for orbit models as value estimation on subgroup lattices, with computable bounds, certified training targets and a lattice version of Monte Carlo tree search.
item.dc:creator: Romie Banerjee

item.title: Risk-Calibrated Intent Routing for Conversational AI via Signed Lexical Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2610.00262v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conversational AI has become widely used as advances in language models let people find information, get writing help, and ask for practical guidance in their own words. When an assistant handles specific tasks, it must infer what the user wants and decide whether to act on that prediction. A sentence classifier's confidence can miss clues in the wording. We combine the gap between the classifier's two highest scores with signed lexical evidence, a score based on words and short character patterns. The score is positive when those patterns favor the predicted intent and negative when they favor another. We use separate calibration data and a statistical upper bound on the error rate to set the minimum confidence required to accept a request. Across ten runs per dataset, our method reduces the area under the risk-coverage curve, which summarizes error as more requests are accepted, by 15.8%, 15.1%, and 11.8% on BANKING77, CLINC150, and HWU64, respectively, compared with a confidence model that uses only sentence classifier scores. At a 5% error target, the share of accepted requests rises by 1.83 percentage points on BANKING77 and 5.14 points on HWU64. CLINC150 already has near-full coverage at that target. At a 2% target, calibration finds a rule that accepts some requests in all 30 runs. Our contribution is a two-feature confidence model that improves routing by measuring how strongly the wording supports or challenges the original intent prediction.
item.dc:creator: Yezhou Cheng, Zehua Yang, Bojun Lin

item.title: CriticHack: Evaluating Visual Rewards Under Robot Policy Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.02527v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learned visual reward models score a robot's execution from camera images and an instruction, and are increasingly used to fine-tune robot policies. Two checks decide whether to trust one: the reward model separates successes from failures, and task success rises during training. We show that both checks can pass while the policy learns to act on the wrong object. When a diffusion policy is fine-tuned against the reward model Robometer to open a drawer, task success rises by 10.2 percentage points. Wrong-object failures, which open a different drawer, rise by 10.9 points, whereas the same training on the simulator's task-completion signal raises success alone. A second reward model, RoboReward-8B, behaves the same way, and the effect reappears on a physical robot. This happens because of how the reward scores the policy's own failures. Most failures make little progress and score low, while a wrong-object failure looks like progress and scores well above them. Optimization shifts a policy toward outcomes that score above the executions they compete with, the executions they can take the place of. It therefore turns low-scoring failures into both successes and wrong-object failures, even when the reward model scores successes higher. This rule needs only executions of the initial policy, so it can be tested before training. On a stacking task we predicted which of three object placements Robometer would exploit, and training raised wrong-object stacks from 20% to 69% in that placement and in neither of the others. The same rule gives a check to run before optimization and a repair that needs no labels: scoring each execution again on frames re-rendered with the objects the instruction does not name put back removes the amplification on both tasks and on the robot.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxuan Luo, Xingguo Xu, Shanshan Wang, Yuhan Zhou, Zhen Zhang

item.title: CAPTOR: a vision-language foundation model for Chest-Abdomen-Pelvis Oncologic CT
item.description: arXiv:2610.14226v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Objectives: Radiologists interpreting oncologic chest-abdomen-pelvis (CAP) CT must also detect non-oncologic conditions, yet existing CT foundation models are trained on single anatomical regions or on non-oncologic data. We developed and evaluated CAPTOR, a vision-language foundation model for oncologic CAP CT that uses an anatomically structured preprocessing strategy to learn from whole examinations. Materials & Methods: CAPTOR is a contrastive vision-language model pretrained on 25,512 predominantly oncologic CAP CT-report pairs (single or multiple series) from a retrospective multicenter dataset (North America, Europe, Asia). It was compared with five CT foundation models, a larger-scale variant (CAPTOR-100K) and an ablation without anatomical preprocessing (CAPTOR-NoPre) on classification and retrieval using held-out internal and public test sets, and on survival prediction using TumorImagingBench. Confidence intervals and pairwise comparisons used patient-level bootstrap and permutation tests. Results: On 10,794 test studies, CAPTOR achieved higher AUC than all five models on CAP (0.767 vs. 0.695 for the next-best model; p<0.001) and oncologic subsets (0.784 vs. 0.734; p<0.001), with superior retrieval on both, and ranked first on three of four oncologic survival benchmarks. Despite substantially fewer training examinations, it performed comparably to CAPTOR-100K. Removing the anatomically structured preprocessing reduced classification performance, including on the institutionally held-out test subset (macro-AUC 0.737 vs. 0.691 for CAPTOR-NoPre, p<0.01). Conclusion: Anatomically structured preprocessing enabled whole-examination CAP CT interpretation, including multiple-series acquisitions, and improved downstream performance. CAPTOR outperformed state-of-the-art CT foundation models on CAP and oncologic subsets while matching a substantially larger-scale variant.
item.dc:creator: S\'el\'ena Jean-Mactoux, Sophie Loizillon, Ghina Jardali, Amandine Cromb\'e, Nathalie Lassau, Alexandre B\^one

item.title: Interaction-as-a-Judge
item.description: arXiv:2610.17895v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coding agents are tasked with producing sophisticated interactive applications such as websites, desktop applications, and games. While humans assess these applications interactively, current automated LLM evaluations primarily focus on code analysis and unit tests. This mismatch can cause LLM judges to miss failures that are immediately apparent to human users. We study Interaction-as-a-Judge, an evaluation paradigm where computer-use agents (CUAs) directly interact with an application. We demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can improve both evaluation and generation of interactive applications. To this end, we collect and release two complementary datasets: $6,858$ pairs of applications with human preferences and corresponding agent traces, and $222$ applications with human-verified requirement labels. Relative to standard non-interactive approaches, we find that Interaction-as-a-Judge improves evaluation in terms of predicting human preferences ($65.6\% \to 69.1\%$) and requirement verification ($77.0\% \to 81.6\%$). We also observe scaling benefits: across both preference alignment and requirement verification, higher-quality interactions improve performance. Finally, through both inference- and training-time experiments, we demonstrate that Interaction-as-a-Judge can also improve the quality of generated artifacts. At inference time, Interaction-as-a-Judge repairs $75.5\%$ of broken requirements within five attempts, compared to $55.4\%$ for code-only self-feedback. At training time, using Interaction-as-a-Judge as a reward signal improves win-rate over the base model by $6.7$pp while reducing both generated code length by $35.7\%$ and build failure rates by $7.2$pp compared to a code-only reward signal.
item.dc:creator: Wayne Chi, I-Hung Hsu, Li Chen, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ion Stoica, Anastasios Nikolas Angelopoulos, Ameet Talwalkar, Chris Donahue, Cho-Jui Hsieh

item.title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds
item.description: arXiv:2610.23297v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. Users compare focal choices on one photograph, so content stability across edits matters alongside quality and speed. Recent generative methods rerun large diffusion models for every edit, even when they first restore an all-in-focus image, so content can change inconsistently between edits. Yet only this restoration is highly ill-posed and benefits from a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders each edit with a lightweight network. A one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and defocus-bias attention to promote information exchange between tokens with similar blur magnitudes. Because every edit reuses the same reconstruction, in-focus content stays consistent across edits, and editing the map enables tilt-shift and two-plane effects. We further collect 3CReal, a benchmark of 89 pairs from three camera-lens systems, to evaluate generalization to unseen optics. For zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal, FlashReFocus leads the evaluated methods in fidelity and perceptual quality. At 1536x1536, a complete refocus takes 2.45 s and each subsequent edit 0.46 s on one RTX PRO 6000.
item.dc:creator: Ching-Heng Cheng, Chia-Ming Lee, Ming-Ching Chang, Xin Li, Chih-Chung Hsu

item.title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.26651v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Maiwald, Roderick McNeill, Jaeyoung Lee, Matthew A. Clarke, Lennart Justen, Alejandro Acelas, Ivo Andrews, Giles Harper-Donnelly, Adam Moore, Sophie Rose, Oliver M. Crook, Felix Jackson

item.title: The Digital-Energy Recomposition of the Kitchin Cycle: Exploratory Evidence from U.S. IT and Irish Data-Centre Series (1995-2025)
item.description: arXiv:2610.33122v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Using quarterly FRED and CSO Ireland data over 1995Q1-2025Q4, we examine whether U.S.\ IT investment and Irish data-centre electricity are recomposing the Kitchin cycle around energy- and compute-backed assets. Three findings stand out. First, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test locates a significant break in the U.S.\ IT-GDP correlation at 2014Q3 (sup-W $= 9.69$; $r$ falls from $+0.45$ to $-0.12$); the Fisher $r$-to-$z$ test survives Bonferroni adjustment ($z = +3.11$, $p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.006$), whereas the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI boundary does not ($p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.164$), so ``Strategic Decoupling'' pre-dates the AI Era by approximately six years. Second, in Ireland the synchronous AI-Era correlation between metered data-centre electricity and Real GDP is large ($r = +0.41$, $N = 16$) but \emph{collapses to $r \approx 0$ when Real GDP is replaced by Real GNP}, suggesting the headline is largely an artefact of the shared multinational tax-structure footprint between hyperscaler operations and Irish gross output. Third, the Irish cross-correlation profile is asymmetric in the opposite direction to a leading-indicator reading: the largest positive coefficients cluster on the $k < 0$ side (GDP precedes data-centre load), so compute capacity is better read as coincident or moderately lagging. Given the small AI-Era samples and the absence of a quarterly multinational-adjusted aggregate such as GNI*, all coefficients are exploratory; subject to these caveats, the U.S.\ Kitchin cycle is best dated to 2014Q3, and the Irish Energy-Data Nexus is dominated by multinational firm activity.
item.dc:creator: Bartosz Zi\'o{\l}ko, Adam Niedzialkowski, Bartosz Szyma

item.title: Practical Assessment of Agentic Systems in Acoustics
item.description: arXiv:2610.39685v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In engineering, applications of artificial intelligence have so far been largely limited to surrogate models and optimization tasks. Large language models changed this, as they can write software from a task given in words. Placed inside a harness, a system of components that lets it search for information and execute software, such a model becomes an agent that can take over recurring engineering tasks. This work measures how the model and the elements of the harness shape the performance and behavior of the agent in two common acoustic applications. In the first application, the agent detects and locates faults in audio recordings from a vehicle interior with near-perfect accuracy. A benchmark on this task shows that a weak model sets a limit that no harness design can overcome, and that design choices take effect only once the model is capable enough to use them. In the second application, a case study on the design of a metamaterial unit cell, the agent reliably finds designs that achieve a specified insertion loss over a given frequency range. The results aim to help the reader understand what each element of an agent contributes and how to design an agent for acoustic tasks.
item.dc:creator: Arne Hildenbrand, Philipp Diel, Zhuo Cao, Hanno Scharr, Marco G\"unther, Stefan Pischinger, Steffen Marburg

item.title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?
item.description: arXiv:2611.00515v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.
item.dc:creator: Zeyu Liu, Sing Kwong Lai, Xuanzhi Feng, HaoYang Shang, Yang Li, Zihao Fang, Xuan Liu, Song Guo

item.title: PhoneValue-Bench: A Dual-Ground-Truth Scorecard Benchmark for Smartphone Recommerce Inspection
item.description: arXiv:2611.00791v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Remote smartphone recommerce is scaling quickly, and locking a repurchase offer from seller photos and diagnostic screens before the handset arrives has become a central operational task. Existing multimodal resources mainly target defect localization, catalog attributes, or screen reading. They overlook payout-facing scorecards with dual cosmetic and operational ground truth under a declared input contract. This gap stems from two challenges: (1) the lack of a large weakly labeled trade-in corpus kept separate from a compact audited ranking cut, and (2) architectures that either flatten unordered photo bags into one prompt or collapse evaluation into a single price scalar. To address these challenges, we propose PhoneValue-Bench, a dual-ground-truth recommerce framework with PhoneValue-Corpus for weak training on 21,550 orders and 278,748 images, and PV-Rank as the only leaderboard on 335 quality-gated orders. Systems are ranked by CardScore under LeadGate, with Cosmetic Fill and Operational Fill as diagnostics, while grade and price stay off the board. Notably, ValueAgent is a six-stage perception-fusion reference that canonicalizes views, detects regional defects, reads screenshots, and fuses evidence under warehouse-style rules, so bag-of-images prompting is not the only evaluation unit. On the same PV-Rank cut and frozen scorer, this full-system and input-contract comparison finds ValueAgent at 84.1 CardScore against the strongest Flat Vision-Language Model at 69.9, with the largest reported gap in CosFill, while OpsFill remains limited under the two declared contracts. CardScore measures field-fill completeness, not quote accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Deng, Chuanzhi Xu, Junjie Huang, Xiaozhen Zhong, Du Tiantian

item.title: GSExplorer: Interactive World Generation with a Persistent 3DGS World State
item.description: arXiv:2611.01543v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interactive world generation requires both accurate local control and stable scene consistency over long rollouts. Existing methods improve local generation through camera or geometry conditioning and extend historical context with memory mechanisms. However, long-horizon exploration remains challenging due to incomplete target-view guidance and inconsistencies accumulated during scene updates. We present \textbf{GSExplorer}, a generation--reconstruction framework built around a persistent 3D Gaussian world state. At each step, the current 3DGS scene provides multimodal rendering conditions for a video generator, while camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch. Generated videos are then fed back to a SLAM-based reconstruction backend, where appearance and geometric consistency checks produce a shared support mask for selective scene updates and cross-chunk pose refinement. We further design a data-construction pipeline that reproduces realistic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation, yielding 293K training pairs of degraded multimodal renderings and real target videos. GSExplorer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on both single-step and three-step WorldScore evaluation, including a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation. On 481-frame leave-and-return rollouts, it also shows strong revisit consistency.
item.dc:creator: Sicheng Yu, Liu Liu, Xinjie Wang, Xinjiang Wang, Taojun Ding, Wenhao Hu, Beizhen Zhao, Puxin Yan, Zhizhong Su, Hao Wang

item.title: FusionCLIP: Multimodal Contrastive Pretraining for Fusion Plasma Diagnostics
item.description: arXiv:2611.09493v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Visible-light videos and multivariate diagnostic signals provide complementary observations of tokamak discharges. However, existing fusion pretraining methods primarily learn representations by reconstructing or predicting observations, leaving the correspondence between these modalities underexplored. Representation learning is further challenged by spatially localized plasma regions in video frames and substantial differences in diagnostic sampling rates. We propose FusionCLIP, a multimodal contrastive pretraining framework. A selective video encoder retains informative visual tokens, while a query-based time-series encoder integrates asynchronous diagnostic signals using their observation timestamps. Contrastive learning aligns representations of the two modalities. We construct the EAST Multimodal Diagnostics (EAST-MMD) dataset, comprising 1307 EAST discharges, and evaluate the model through independent fine-tuning on three tasks: disruption prediction, edge-localized mode (ELM) classification, and H98 regression. FusionCLIP achieves a Joint score of 89.07%, with absolute gains of 2.41% and 2.90% over the best competing baseline, and the in-domain contrastive pretraining baseline CLIP-Base, respectively. Ablations and attention visualizations further support the contributions of its key components.
item.dc:creator: Qiang Chen, Xiao Wang, Qingquan Yang, Hao Si, Zikang Yan, Guosheng Xu, Jin Tang

item.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
item.description: arXiv:2611.09892v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
item.dc:creator: Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jean-Baptiste Regli, Kejia Ren, Petr \v{S}vec, David J. Yoon, Matthias M\"uller, Vladlen Koltun

item.title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.10592v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, outperforming frontier VLM judges by 4.4%-12.8% while achieving at least 90% recall for both human approvals and rejections. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 5.0% to 68.0%. Across 15 models at their highest reasoning effort, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We fine-tune Qwen3.8-27B with group relative policy optimization (GRPO) using our verification programs as rewards, improving pass@1 from 30.31% to 52.19% on held-out instances. Our project page is at https://motion-graphics-bench.github.io/.
item.dc:creator: Jiaju Ma, Ashvini Kumar Jindal, Chuhua Wang, Sumithra Bhakthavatsalam

item.title: How Path Integral Diffusion Decides a Finite Spin Glass
item.description: arXiv:2611.11826v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When an AI diffusion-type generator samples a frustrated spin glass, which macroscopic alternatives does it decide first, and when? We study this for bridge-diffusion models of the Path Integral Diffusion (PID) type started from a point source. We show that every isotropic PID is a time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, and conversely every signal-to-noise schedule is realized by a PID protocol. What a continuous-time generator decides therefore does not depend on the protocol, which only sets when and at what cost. We describe the generator's state by its partial commitments: the probabilities it assigns, at each moment, to nested classes of configurations fixed by the target. The partial commitments are martingales that move only along class contrasts. Their ensemble average gives the information about each level at an exact rate set by squared magnetization contrasts. In the balanced, effectively binary approximation, a split reaches half of its class information near \gamma=1.044/\lambda_P, where \lambda_P is the leading eigenvalue of the parent covariance. The theory is applied to Bethe-lattice and Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) glasses with up to 24 spins. It is observed generically that a trajectory first shifts its weight to one of the two mirror halves of the zero-field measure and then to the glassy classes inside it. These classes appear near the glass transition, keep their identity on cooling and are absent in a ferromagnet on the same graphs. Sparse (Bethe) and dense (SK) glasses differ in how often and how strongly such classes exist, not in how trajectories commit to them. For a generator that takes finitely many steps, the protocol matters through the late, local stage rather than the macroscopic decisions. Sampled posteriors at N=32,64 and small trained denoisers show the same sequence.
item.dc:creator: Michael Chertkov

item.title: 2D Gum-Net: Unsupervised Dense Elastic Image Registration via Symmetric Correlation and Spectral Pooling
item.description: arXiv:2611.12805v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Dense non-rigid registration, the recovery of a pixel-wise deformation field that warps one image into geometric agreement with another, is fundamental across medical imaging, structural biology, and correspondence estimation, yet learning-based approaches face a severe bottleneck: ground-truth deformation fields are notoriously difficult to obtain for real data. We present 2D Gum-Net, an end-to-end architecture that predicts dense elastic deformation fields fully unsupervised. We transfer the Geometric Unsupervised Matching Network (Gum-Net), originally developed for 3D subtomogram alignment in cryo-electron tomography, to 2D elastic registration: all three modules are redesigned in 2D, and the rigid transformation head is replaced by a Dense Spatial Transformer that regresses a sparse control-point grid, lifted to a full-resolution field $\Phi$ by bicubic interpolation. Downsampling uses DCT spectral pooling, implemented as frozen-basis matrix multiplications ($\approx 50\times$ GPU speedup), preserving the fine, quasi-periodic structure that max and average pooling destroy. We evaluate on contact-based fingerprints, a challenging testbed for this task: locally self-similar ridge patterns make correspondence maximally ambiguous, skin pressed against a sensor generates authentic large-displacement elastic distortion, and minutiae act as precise landmarks through which an independent matcher externally verifies the topological correctness of predicted fields. Trained purely on synthetic impressions and evaluated zero-shot on real benchmarks, our method improves structural correlation by up to 15.7% on FVC2004 and raises genuine match scores under an independent matcher while leaving imposter scores essentially unchanged. This suggests that the predicted deformations restore true structure without fabricating correspondences.
item.dc:creator: Aarya Bhave, Anushka Ajay Bhave

item.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
item.description: arXiv:2611.15108v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of a claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks normalization and makes algorithmic conversion non-transitive. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($irrel : \Pi P{:}Prop.\,\Pi p,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, $\Pi$-covariant subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, compile to unification-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$), and match declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) for open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.
item.dc:creator: Hans-Martin Will

item.title: VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender
item.description: arXiv:2611.15789v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by generating a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these rendered proxy videos and the complex, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene generation: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether facts that pass the rules are recognizable in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.
item.dc:creator: Yuzhe Chen, Muxi Diao, Lele Yang, Wenbin Xu, Xuyang Liu, Qile Su, Changyi Liu, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Jiale Cao

item.title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
item.description: arXiv:2611.18397v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.
item.dc:creator: Run Luo, Kuan Zhang, Qi Deng, Yukun Chen, Zhihao Yang, Yufei Zhang, Renrong Hu, Yi Zhang, Guiyu Ma, Tianyu Fan, Longze Chen, Hao Sun, Jiaming Li, Jiaming Yang, Xiaohao Liu, Tao Tan, Minzheng Wang, Hangtian Jia, Shuai Yuan, Lvdi Wang, Xiao Liu, Chao Ma, Yuting Zou, Yinhe Zheng, Xiaobo Xia, Dawei Jiang, Shaoqing Ren

item.title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
item.description: arXiv:2611.20011v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain.
item.dc:creator: Nikos Theodoridis, Reenu Mohandas, Sushil Sharma, Ciar\'an Hogan, Ganesh Sistu, Anthony Scanlan, Tim Brophy, Ciar\'an Eising

item.title: Markets for Compute and Inference: Structure, Financing, and Risk Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.20242v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Capacity to run large language models is rented by the accelerator-hour, and their output is sold by the million tokens. Both goods now have published price indices, an over-the-counter forward has traded on one, compute futures are listed offshore, and CME and ICE have specified futures on rental indices that await the United States regulator. We ask what in these two markets can be hedged, by whom, and at what price. Three findings stand out. First, the price that exchange contracts settle on is not the price that drives operators' revenue. The contracts on CME and ICE reference published short-dated rental rates, while most revenue, and with it credit quality, comes from private multi-year contracts whose prices are largely undisclosed. Second, the token price and the rental rate are linked by an identity through throughput and margin, but they are different exposures, so a hedge on the rental rate does not hedge the cost of inference; at the measured capability of GPT-5 the cheapest list price fell by a factor of 17 in twelve months, and by far less at lower capability. Third, the demand for hedging already sits in credit agreements, as the years by which operators' debt outlives their contracted revenue. Filings cannot measure that gap, because debt is scheduled year by year while contracted revenue rarely is, and the one loan that prices it settles the risk by cash prepayment against a model only the parties see. We design a reverse convertible note through which leveraged operators could buy protection against falling rental rates. Its coupon depends steeply on the annualised volatility of the rental rate, which the two public indices put between about 5% and 89% according to how each is built and the horizon measured; across that range the fair one-year coupon runs from 4.1% to 31.6%.
item.dc:creator: Dr Gabriel Borrageiro

item.title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
item.description: arXiv:2611.20811v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds, and merchants order stock and plan promotions on that lift. We show that an explanation can pass the checks used to trust it and still be wrong enough to cost money. We define eight checks for any forecaster that states a plan lift, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and run them on a world model and on LightGBM. In generated store data with known effects, the world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet when merchants plan into high-demand weeks it states 1.33 to 1.40 times the true lift, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world; LightGBM overstates it too (1.26, and 1.16 to 1.35). Both still pick the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to the world model's lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. The world model's stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, an error in kind that only a measured cause finds. Sanity checks for explanations test whether an explanation depends on the model; a decision needs to know whether it is right about the world, and these results show the first does not give the second. For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan on every window, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05). A noisy benchmark of price episodes in Dominick's data is reported as a check of direction only.
item.dc:creator: Karthik Iyer

item.title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics
item.description: arXiv:2611.22268v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.
item.dc:creator: John P. Nelson

item.title: MAVE: Reconstructing Editable 3D Blockouts from Film Shots
item.description: arXiv:2611.22464v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Animated 3D blockouts support previsualization and provide structural conditions for video generation, but manually reconstructing them from reference videos is costly. This limits both their use by creators and the production of paired training data. We introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark of 50 film shots and 416 keyframes for evaluating camera motion, spatial layout, and character blocking. We propose MAVE, a video-to-blockout framework combining Metric observation, Agentic modeling, and evidence-based VErification. It first recovers cameras, human motion, and geometric evidence in a shared metric coordinate system. An agent then constructs an editable environment under constraints from these observations, while programmatic checks report inconsistencies to guide refinement. The outputs are editable Blender scenes and frame-aligned blockout videos. On MAVEBench, MAVE improves overall scores by 27.5-41.1 points across three agents over their corresponding vanilla baselines. With DeepSeek-1017, it achieves a score of 73.2 at an average API cost of only USD 0.054 per shot, outperforming the strongest vanilla baseline while reducing total reconstruction time by 53%. We also construct MAVEData-3K, a dataset of 3,000 blockout-video pairs for model training, and will release it publicly. Creators can change viewpoints and character paths, then render the edited scenes to condition video generation. Code is available at https://github.com/yfChang-cv/MAVE.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Chang, Jian Yang, Jiangnan Shao, Xiaofeng Wang, Zhaoxin Fan, Renjing Xu, Ming Lu, Xingang Wang, Zheng Zhu

item.title: Hierarchical Control of Antiphase Synchronization in Biomorphic Spiking Neural Architectures for Locomotor Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.22639v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Central pattern generators (CPGs) provide a biologically inspired foundation for adaptive locomotor control, yet systematically characterizing their dynamic regimes in spiking neural networks remains challenging. This study introduces a framework for identifying and stabilizing antiphase synchronization in a biomorphic spiking CPG model embedded in a closed neuromuscular loop. A composite synchronization metric is developed, integrating phase coherence, amplitude balance, and temporal stability. Its performance is evaluated across systematically varied stimulation waveforms and synaptic configurations. Statistical analysis reveals that stimulation type dominates regime determination, with tonic drive yielding the most robust antiphase synchronization. Periodic inputs induce nonlinear saturation and context-dependent network routing. Although synaptic weights alone show limited discriminative power, they significantly modulate robustness within a given stimulation context, with reciprocal Ia interneuron connections emerging as key stabilizers. The proposed composite metric achieves robust antiphase detection, outperforming traditional phase-only measures while preserving biophysical interpretability. These findings establish a statistically validated, hierarchical modeling approach in which external drive defines the operating regime and targeted synaptic configurations fine-tune dynamic stability, providing actionable guidelines for closed-loop neuromechanical controllers and adaptive neuroprosthetic interfaces.
item.dc:creator: Artem Guba, Nikolay Kovalev, Alexey Zharinov, Vacheslav Demin, Viktor B. Kazantsev

item.title: Check Your Blind Spots: Decision-Guided Perception by Probing the Planner with Hypothetical Objects
item.description: arXiv:2611.23030v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Not every perception error changes the planner's action. Yet adaptive-resolution perception chooses where to spend high-resolution computation from image cues, which can neither reliably point to an object that low resolution missed nor tell which objects matter to the planner. We observe that the planner can say where an object would matter before anything is seen: inserting a hypothetical object at a location tests whether its action would change. Decision-Guided Speculative Perception (DGSP) treats the low-resolution scene and its action as a draft and probes the planner in this way to obtain a decision-sensitivity field, the locations where an unseen object would change the action. Only this field and the support, the detections on which the current action rests, are verified at high resolution, repeatedly until the action is stable. For two planner classes, we prove that DGSP returns exactly the action of whole-frame high-resolution perception if crop detections match whole-frame ones and the crops cover the field, conditions that real images meet approximately. On three driving datasets, it reproduces this action on about 98% of frames with about a quarter of the pixels. At the pixel cost of uniform downscaling, it repairs more of the draft's disagreements with this action, brakes falsely less often, and recovers many more of the decision-relevant objects that the draft misses.
item.dc:creator: Hoang Pham Cong, Long D. Nguyen, Ho Viet Duc Luong, Nguyen Tran Minh Nhat, Binh P. Nguyen
